Summarise backtest scores

Source: R/eval-backtest.R
mt_score.Rd

Summarise backtest scores

Usage

mt_score(
  backtest,
  by = "model",
  target = c("rate", "life_expectancy", "asr", "life_expectancy_gap", "asr_gap"),
  measures = NULL
)

Arguments

backtest

An mt_backtest() result (or several combined with rbind()).

by

Grouping columns, for example c("model", "horizon").

target

"rate" (log death rates per cell, default), "life_expectancy" or "asr" (when the backtest scored these quantities, see quantities in mt_backtest()), or "life_expectancy_gap" or "asr_gap" (differences between strata, see contrast in mt_backtest()).

measures

Optional further summaries (none by default):

  • "sape": the mean standardised absolute predictive error of Raftery et al. (2013), sqrt(pi / 2) |y - median| / sd with the standard deviation sd of the predictive draws. It is scaled so that its expected value is 1 when the predictive distribution is correct and normal; a mean above 1 indicates intervals that are too narrow, below 1 too wide. Raftery et al. define it for life expectancy, so it is available for target = "life_expectancy" only. Rows whose draws have no spread (sd = 0) are left out;

  • "cov90": the empirical coverage of the central 90% intervals. Raftery et al. (2013) report the coverage of the 80%, 90% and 95% intervals with their mean half-widths; with by = c("model", "horizon") they are given by horizon;

  • "halfwidth": the mean half-widths hw80, hw90, hw95 of these intervals (Raftery et al. 2013, Table 1);

  • "revision": the mean absolute revision, the absolute change of the forecast median of a cell (stratum, age group, year) between consecutive origins of the backtest, for every cell forecast from both. It is a summary of this package (reference unknown). Stoeldraijer et al. (2013) name robustness as a purpose of a forecast: small changes in the observations when the data are updated should result in only modest changes in the forecasts. A revision belongs to the later origin and its horizon; the first origin has none. Origins further apart than one year (for example origins = c(2005, 2007)) give revisions over several years of data. The published measure of robustness is "robustness";

  • "robustness": the robustness of Stoeldraijer et al. (2018), "the standard deviation (SD) of the increase/decrease" of the forecast of one target year over successive forecasts, each with one more year of data; a lower standard deviation means a more robust forecast. They forecast life expectancy at age 65 in 2020 from the fitting periods 1960-2005, ..., 1960-2014. Here, for each cell (stratum, age group, target year and target), it is the sample standard deviation (stats::sd()) of the revisions of the forecast median between consecutive origins (as for "revision"), for cells with at least two revisions (NA otherwise); the column robustness is the mean of these standard deviations over the cells of a group, each cell counted once. With one stratum, target = "life_expectancy" and one target year (by = c("model", "period")) this is the published measure; the mean over several cells is package-specific (reference unknown). The revisions of a cell span several origins and horizons, so by cannot contain "horizon" or "origin": group by the target year ("period"). The target years of a backtest are observed years, so the origins and h must reach them from every origin: for example origins = 2005:2014 and h = 10 forecast 2015 from all ten origins, one year apart like the fitting periods of the paper. The life expectancy of a backtest is that at the first age of the grid, so at age 65 for data from age 65.

Value

A data.table with the mean CRPS, WIS and absolute error, the root mean squared error of the median (rmse), MASE (mean of absolute error over the scale, the mean absolute year-to-year change of the training data, as the mean absolute scaled error of Hyndman and Koehler 2006; rates only), empirical coverage of the 50%, 80% and 95% intervals, mean PIT, the number of scored cells (n), the number of them whose observed deaths were floored at half a death (n_floored, see mt_backtest(); NA for targets other than "rate" and for backtest tables without the column floored) and the unit of CRPS, WIS and absolute error (log rates, or years for life expectancy). The scores of floored cells can dominate the means of sparse data; the derived quantities and coarser age groups avoid the floor. Backtests of the same model with different preprocessing (column prep) are scored separately. With measures, the columns sape, cov90, hw80, hw90, hw95, revision and robustness follow.

References

Hyndman RJ, Koehler AB (2006). Another look at measures of forecast accuracy. International Journal of Forecasting 22(4): 679-688.

Raftery AE, Chunn JL, Gerland P, Sevcikova H (2013). Bayesian probabilistic projections of life expectancy for all countries. Demography 50(3): 777-801. doi:10.1007/s13524-012-0193-x

Stoeldraijer L, van Duin C, van Wissen L, Janssen F (2013). Impact of different mortality forecasting methods and explicit assumptions on projected future life expectancy: the case of the Netherlands. Demographic Research 29(13): 323-354. doi:10.4054/DemRes.2013.29.13

Stoeldraijer L, van Duin C, van Wissen L, Janssen F (2018). Comparing strategies for matching mortality forecasts to the most recently observed data: exploring the trade-off between accuracy and robustness. Genus 74: 16. doi:10.1186/s41118-018-0041-y

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1990:2012)
bt <- mt_backtest(rwd(), x, origins = 2007, h = 5, n_draws = 100)
mt_score(bt, by = c("model", "horizon"))
#>                     model horizon       crps        wis        mae       rmse
#>                    <char>   <num>      <num>      <num>      <num>      <num>
#> 1: Random walk with drift       1 0.04454219 0.03992641 0.06272241 0.09469268
#> 2: Random walk with drift       2 0.04654157 0.04148880 0.06166271 0.09425197
#> 3: Random walk with drift       3 0.05565911 0.04972059 0.07710375 0.11415199
#> 4: Random walk with drift       4 0.05812890 0.05190181 0.07358098 0.11643492
#> 5: Random walk with drift       5 0.06429823 0.05740455 0.08308110 0.12352441
#>        mase     cov50     cov80     cov95  pit_mean     n n_floored     unit
#>       <num>     <num>     <num>     <num>     <num> <int>     <int>   <char>
#> 1: 1.048261 0.4859155 0.7253521 0.8661972 0.5020423   142         0 log rate
#> 2: 1.157779 0.6126761 0.8591549 0.9718310 0.5157746   142         0 log rate
#> 3: 1.386932 0.6478873 0.8943662 0.9647887 0.4927465   142         0 log rate
#> 4: 1.287454 0.7183099 0.9577465 1.0000000 0.4763380   142         0 log rate
#> 5: 1.459025 0.7605634 0.9507042 1.0000000 0.4895070   142         0 log rate
# life expectancy: SAPE and 90% coverage by horizon (Raftery et al. 2013),
# revisions between consecutive origins
bl <- mt_backtest(rwd(), x, origins = 2004:2007, h = 5, n_draws = 100,
                  quantities = "life_expectancy")
mt_score(bl, by = c("model", "horizon"), target = "life_expectancy",
         measures = c("sape", "cov90", "revision"))

# robustness (Stoeldraijer et al. 2018) of each target year: 2008 and
# 2009 are forecast from all four origins
mt_score(bl, by = c("model", "period"), target = "life_expectancy",
         measures = "robustness")
